title: Online job platforms: choosing and setting up a profile
audience: Owners of small Australian property trade businesses deciding whether an online job platform is worth the time and cost
learningOutcomes: Compare online job platforms on fees, lead quality, contract terms and the time each one needs.
Write a profile with accurate business details, evidence of work and a clear service description.
Measure the cost of each platform lead and decide whether to keep, change or stop using each platform.

instruction.heading: Deciding whether the time is worth it
instruction.body: Online platforms connect people who need work with tradespeople who respond to their requests. They can provide steady leads, but they also bring competition, lead fees, subscriptions and the time spent on bids that never turn into jobs. The guide this lesson draws on names several US sites. Those sites are not Australian services, and their fees and terms are not used here. Before joining any platform, find out whether it operates in the owner's area, what it charges, whether the charge is per lead, per job or by subscription, how it ranks profiles, and what its terms say about contact details. Check each point on the platform's own terms page.

instruction.heading: Building the profile around evidence
instruction.body: A profile is often the first contact a client has with the business. Include the trading name and the owner's name as the owner presents them to the public, the suburbs or regions served, the locations travelled to for work, the specialities, and the website if there is one. Add photos of the owner's own completed work, with client consent. Show a rate or a range if the platform allows it. Write a short description covering what the business does well, how quickly it responds and how it adapts to a client's needs. Ask a friend or family member to read it back. Every licence or insurance claim must match what the owner holds and can show.

instruction.heading: Testing with a small number of platforms
instruction.body: Start with one or two platforms and a fixed trial period. Record every lead, bid, reply, job and invoice against the platform it came from. At the end of the trial, calculate the cost of each lead and the cost per job won, including the time spent bidding. Keep the platforms that produce jobs at an acceptable cost, and stop the rest. Ask each completed client for a review where the platform allows it and the client is willing to give one.

instruction.heading: Protecting client information
instruction.body: Client contact details and addresses are personal information. Do not share them outside the platform, do not post them publicly, and do not contact a client through a channel the platform prohibits. Read the platform's privacy statement before uploading any client photo or detail. Keep the profile details consistent across platforms, so clients do not see conflicting information.

procedure: Check the platform's service area, fees, contract terms and privacy statement on its own site.
Write a profile with accurate business details, service areas, specialities, photos of the owner's own work and a short description.
Check each licence or insurance claim against the evidence held in the business file.
Trial one or two platforms for a fixed period, and record each lead, bid, job and invoice.
Calculate the cost per lead and the cost per job won, including the time spent bidding.
Keep, change or stop each platform, and record the decision and its date.

workedExamples.situation: A platform charges a fee for each lead. The owner has bid on ten leads over six weeks and won one job.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the owner keep paying for leads on this platform?
workedExamples.reasoning: The owner should add up the lead fees and the time spent on bids, then compare the total with the income from the one job. If the cost per job won is more than the owner can absorb at the rate set in “Setting your hourly rate and minimum charge”, the owner should pause the platform or improve the profile first. The decision should be recorded with the figures used.

equipmentAndPpe: Platform trial log with leads, bids, jobs, fees and time spent
Photos of the owner's own completed work, with client consent
Business details sheet with licence and insurance evidence

commonErrors.error: Joining several platforms at once and losing track of the leads and their costs.
commonErrors.prevention: Trial one or two platforms for a fixed period, and record every lead.

commonErrors.error: Writing profile claims about licences, insurance or qualifications the owner does not hold.
commonErrors.prevention: Check every claim against the business file before publishing it.

commonErrors.error: Sharing client details on a public profile or outside the platform.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep client details private, and use only the platform's own channel.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Check them on each platform's own pages before joining.

Listing a licensed service on a platform is a claim about the business. It does not grant a licence, and each licensed task must be held or referred, as “Business registration and licence checks by state and territory” explains.
Consumer law applies to advertising claims and to quotes under the Australian Consumer Law.

qualityStandard: Each platform trial has a fixed period, and its cost per lead and per job won is recorded.
Every profile claim is backed by evidence held in the business file.
No client's personal details are posted publicly or shared outside the platform.
documentationEvidence: Platform comparison table with fees, terms and privacy points checked on each platform's own site
Trial log with leads, bids, jobs, fees and time spent
Profile text and records of client consent for any photo
summary: Check fees, terms and service areas before joining any platform.
Write profile claims that match the evidence the owner holds.
Keep the platforms that produce jobs at a cost the owner can afford.

knowledgeChecks.question: How should an owner judge whether an online platform is worth using?
options: By the number of other tradespeople listed on it and how many of them have reviews
By the cost per job won, including the time spent bidding, over a fixed trial
By the size of the platform's logo and the colour and font of its banner
By whether a guide mentioned the platform and how often it is in the news

knowledgeChecks.question: Which profile statement is acceptable?
options: A licence the owner has not yet obtained and the owner will get it soon
An insurance cover the owner has checked and holds, with the certificate on file
A review copied from another tradesperson with the name changed slightly
A client's full home address shown in the advert to attract enquiries

knowledgeChecks.question: What does the guide's list of US platforms mean for an Australian owner?
options: Those platforms should be joined immediately without checking their terms, fees, reach or any local rules at all
Those platforms are not Australian recommendations; the owner must check which platforms operate locally and their terms
Only US platforms are allowed to advertise handyman work in Australia, and only through a US agent
The list shows the fees for every platform in Australia and the fees are the same for every trade

officialReferences.title: Advertising and selling guide: A guide for business
officialReferences.covers: Read via summary tool (first 100,000 of about 123,600 characters): businesses must not mislead or deceive in advertising, including online and social media content, and the test is the overall impression created. On pricing, the guide says to state the total price, including mandatory fees and taxes, before the customer agrees. The guide does not address quotes or estimates directly. Publisher: Australian Competition and Consumer Commission. Platform-specific rules remain UNCONFIRMED.
